title: The five issues to watch at next month’s IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings
gist: Ahead of the IMF-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, global current account imbalances have widened to roughly 3.6 percent of world GDP, global public debt has hit a record $102 trillion or 91 percent of GDP, and geoeconomic fragmentation could cost up to 7 percent of global GDP. Structural public debt is pushing bond yields higher and posing a major risk to equity markets, while AI is simultaneously the productivity hope and, per Fitch, a correction risk given elevated tech valuations alongside debt accumulation.

insights.claim: Global imbalances measured as the sum of absolute current account surpluses and deficits rose from around 2.4 percent of global GDP in 2019 to around 3.6 percent in 2025, reversing much of the decline from the 2008 peak of almost 6 percent and approaching their highest levels in 150 years.
insights.so_what: Wide imbalances in a low-trust geopolitical setting are the raw material for tariff and capital-control escalation — a persistent FX and trade-policy risk premium.
insights.locator: 1. Global imbalances are back
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

insights.claim: Structural factors now account for 55 to 60 percent of global imbalances, with policy gaps explaining only the remainder, making the imbalances far harder to unwind through policy adjustment.
insights.so_what: If most of the gap is structural, tariff and exchange-rate remedies will underdeliver — expect repeated policy disappointment on rebalancing.
insights.locator: At the same time, the underlying issue has become harder
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

insights.claim: Growing stocks of net international investment positions mean primary income flows now play a larger role in determining current account balances, and bilateral imbalances rooted in global value chain positions are difficult to unwind once established.
insights.so_what: Current accounts are increasingly driven by asset-income stocks rather than trade flows, so trade policy has less traction on headline balances than assumed.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, growing stocks of net international investment positions
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

insights.claim: The US, China, and Europe together account for one-half to two-thirds of global imbalances, yet the IMF can only identify distortions and recommend policy changes, not compel major economies to act.
insights.so_what: The institution nominally in charge of rebalancing has no enforcement power over the three blocs that matter — do not expect multilateral resolution.
insights.quote: it cannot compel major economies—including the US, China, and Europe, which together account for one-half to two-thirds of global imbalances—to act on its advice
insights.locator: And the IMF has little ability to prevent that outcome.
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

insights.claim: Imbalances rooted in economic fundamentals need not be problematic when countries cooperate and trust one another, but in today's geopolitical climate they are more likely to fuel economic and political friction.
insights.so_what: The danger of an imbalance is a function of political trust, not its size — a useful filter for judging when a deficit becomes a policy flashpoint.
insights.locator: Imbalances rooted in economic fundamentals need not be problematic
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

insights.claim: Since the Russian invasion of Ukraine, trade between geopolitically distant countries fell 12 percent relative to trade within geopolitical blocs, and foreign direct investment between distant countries declined 20 percent.
insights.so_what: Bloc alignment is already repricing cross-border capital allocation — FDI is fragmenting faster than trade, which matters most for greenfield and supply-chain capex.
insights.locator: 2. Geopolitical rivalries are fragmenting trade and investment
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

insights.claim: Protectionist measures such as tariffs reached more than 2,500 actions in 2025, nearly five times the number recorded in 2015.
insights.so_what: A fivefold rise in a decade makes trade-policy risk a permanent cost of doing business rather than an episodic shock.
insights.locator: At the same time, protectionist measures such as tariffs
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

insights.claim: The IMF estimates geoeconomic fragmentation could reduce global GDP by as much as 7 percent.
insights.so_what: Puts a headline number on the cumulative cost of bloc formation — a slow-burn drag on global growth expectations and therefore on long-run earnings.
insights.locator: the IMF estimating that geoeconomic fragmentation could reduce
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

insights.claim: A growing disconnect has opened between the IMF's traditional mandate of promoting balanced growth through productivity and efficiency gains and member states that now weight economic and national security above efficiency and use industrial policy to reduce strategic dependencies.
insights.so_what: Industrial policy is the durable regime, not a detour — capital allocation will keep following security logic even where it is economically inefficient.
insights.locator: More fundamentally, fragmentation has exposed a growing disconnect
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

themes.theme: Record debt and the bond-yield channel

insights.claim: Global public debt has increased to a record $102 trillion, or 91 percent of global GDP.
insights.so_what: The level itself is the anchor for any duration view — debt at 91 percent of GDP constrains fiscal response to the next shock.
insights.locator: 3. Debt is squeezing public finances
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

insights.claim: More than 3.4 billion people, or 41 percent of the world's population, live in countries that spend more on interest payments than on education or health care.
insights.so_what: A political-economy tipping point: debt service crowding out core services is the precondition for restructuring pressure and social unrest in EM sovereigns.
insights.locator: Today, more than 3.4 billion people
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

insights.claim: Elevated structural public debt is increasingly putting upward pressure on bond yields, posing a major risk to equity markets and economic prospects.
insights.so_what: The stated transmission channel from fiscal deficits to equity drawdown — long-end yields, not central bank policy rates, are the variable to watch.
insights.quote: elevated structural public debt is increasingly putting upward pressure on bond yields, posing a major risk to equity markets and economic prospects
insights.locator: As a result, elevated structural public debt
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

insights.claim: The debt increase has become structural rather than cyclical, driven by fiscal deficits the IMF estimates will reach 5 percent of global GDP plus pandemic legacy costs and rising spending on defense, climate mitigation, and population aging.
insights.so_what: Structural deficit drivers mean supply of government paper keeps growing regardless of the cycle — a persistent term-premium argument.
insights.locator: The increase in public debt has become increasingly structural
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

insights.claim: Public resistance to higher taxation appears to be spreading globally, reflecting declining trust in governments and making it harder to raise the revenues needed to contain debt.
insights.so_what: Closes off the revenue side of consolidation, leaving inflation, financial repression, or yields as the adjustment valve.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, public resistance to higher taxation
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

themes.theme: Aging, climate, and AI as fiscal pressures

insights.claim: The number of workers paying taxes to support each retiree globally is expected to fall from six in the 1960s to two in 2035, transferring a larger fiscal burden onto working-age populations and potentially intensifying intergenerational tensions.
insights.so_what: A 6-to-2 dependency shift on a nine-year horizon is the hard constraint behind pension reform fights and structurally higher sovereign issuance.
insights.locator: First, demographic change is reshaping public finances.
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

insights.claim: Natural disaster losses totaled $592 billion across 2024 and 2025 combined, while the OECD estimates $5 trillion a year will be needed through 2030 for climate mitigation and the energy transition.
entities: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development
insights.so_what: The gap between realized loss and required investment defines the size of the climate financing shortfall — relevant to insurers, cat bond pricing, and transition capex.
insights.locator: Second, the economic costs of climate change
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

insights.claim: AI is simultaneously a solution and a risk: it could lift productivity and potential growth enough to offset aging and high debt, but also threatens large-scale labor displacement that worsens inequality and triggers social and political backlash even if aggregate prosperity rises.
insights.so_what: The fiscal case for AI depends on whether gains are broadly distributed — political backlash is the transmission channel from AI success to policy risk.
insights.locator: Third, AI offers both a potential solution and a new source of risk.
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

insights.claim: Fitch has warned of an AI market correction given elevated technology-stock valuations alongside substantial debt accumulation, making AI a near-term financial-stability risk and not only a long-run growth question.
insights.so_what: A ratings agency flagging AI valuations plus leverage is the cleanest named catalyst here for a tech drawdown thesis.
insights.quote: Fitch has warned of an AI market correction given elevated technology-stock valuations alongside substantial debt accumulation
insights.locator: In the near term, AI could also create financial-stability risks
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

insights.claim: Record debt and persistent deficits leave countries with less room to respond to demographic aging, climate change, and AI-driven disruption simultaneously.
insights.so_what: Three structural shocks arriving while fiscal space is exhausted is the core reason to expect more market-based adjustment and less policy cushioning.
insights.locator: 4. From AI to aging, new pressures are building
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

themes.theme: K-shaped growth and the development squeeze

insights.claim: AI has contributed to an increasingly K-shaped pattern of economic growth, widening the gap between developed and developing countries because economies with greater access to AI, capital, and advanced technologies are better positioned to capture productivity gains.
insights.so_what: AI adoption capacity becomes a sovereign differentiator — a new axis for EM country selection beyond commodities and rates.
insights.locator: 5. The development divide is widening
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

insights.claim: Official development assistance from developed countries has fallen by almost a third from its 2023 peak to $174.3 billion in 2025, with a further 6.9 percent decline expected this year and no alternative sources offsetting it.
insights.so_what: A one-third collapse in aid flows tightens external financing for frontier sovereigns just as debt service peaks — raises default and restructuring probability.
insights.locator: Making matters worse, official development assistance
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

insights.claim: Geopolitical rivalry has increased mistrust among the IMF's and World Bank's major shareholders, making it difficult to reach consensus on expanding their financial resources to meet rising needs.
insights.so_what: Quota and capital increases are unlikely, capping the multilateral backstop available in the next EM crisis.
insights.locator: The IMF and World Bank must navigate a new reality
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

insights.claim: The challenge for the IMF and World Bank at the Bangkok meetings is not only to mobilize additional resources but to navigate a geopolitical minefield while delivering a focused package of practical assistance to low-income countries.
insights.so_what: Sets a low, concrete bar for the meetings — a focused low-income package rather than systemic reform is the realistic deliverable to watch for.
